\begin{abstract}
In April 2016 a House of Commons committee heard that new television rules from the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) would cost \lttvJobsTotal{} media jobs by 2020. The figure came from a commissioned study detailed enough to check. I fixed the forecast record and analysis plan before collecting outcomes and compared two of the study's three scenarios with CRTC data for 2016--2019. The clearest miss was an input: the study assumed that \lttvByopSixteen{} of subscribers would take the entry-level package in 2016, rising to \lttvByopEighteen{}; the CRTC counted \lttvUptakeJuneShare{} by mid-2016. As planned, specialty and pay channels' revenue, on which most of the job figure depends, was inconsistent with the forecast path at the pre-stated error scale, and distributors' revenue was consistent with it. Analyses added after seeing outcomes found channel revenue consistent with the study's model run at the uptake counted, most of the distributors' shortfall beyond that run, and per-subscriber payments to Canadian channels above the no-reform path. The testimony presented figures resting on the uptake assumption as unconditional job losses, called an economy-wide estimate, more than half of it spin-off, media jobs, and cited a share of programming spending that the study's figures don't reproduce.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} forecast evaluation; ex post analysis; economic impact studies; broadcasting regulation; Canada
